title: Design a UPI payments switch
dek: A payer app sends ₹480 to a shop. The switch sits between two banks it does not run: debit one, credit the other, never take the money twice, and put it back if the second step fails. Salary day sends several times the normal load.

body.x: This is our own model of a payment switch, not a description of how NPCI or any bank builds UPI. The numbers are model figures: we say so each time.

items: Pay: a payer app sends money from one UPI address (VPA) to another, for example ₹480 to Zotato.
Check: if the app times out, it can ask what happened to its payment and always gets one honest answer.
Reverse: if the payer's bank debited but the payee's bank could not credit, the money goes back to the payer.
Never debit twice for the same payment, even if the app, the network or a bank repeats a call.
Salary day (the 1st of the month) and festival sales must not break any of the above.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: One debit per payment; every debit ends as success or reversed, never forgotten
The payer sees success, failed, or "pending, don't pay again"
Starting a payment works even when one bank is slow or down
A model month-start: about 4,000 payments a second at 10 am

items: Model: 10 crore payments a day is about 1,200 a second on average, spread unevenly. Public monthly UPI counts are in the thousands of crores; we use a smaller model so the numbers fit one design.
Salary day is the peak: about 3 to 4 times an ordinary hour, so about 4,000 payments a second at 10 am (model).
Each payment is one row of about 250 bytes: 10 crore a day is about 25 GB a day, kept for years, so it is partitioned by date.
Each payment makes two bank calls (debit, then credit), and banks answer in hundreds of milliseconds: the bank calls, not your servers, set how long a payment takes.
Reversals are rare: perhaps 1 payment in a thousand (model). They must still be exactly right.
Transaction: `txn_id`, `request_id` (from the app, unique), `payer_vpa`, `payee_vpa`, `amount`, `status` (pending, debited, success, failed, reversed), `at`.
Reversal: `reversal_id`, `txn_id`, `amount`, `at`. Only ever added.

body.label: API
body.say: Pay with a request id from the app and get back a pending payment. Ask for its status by the same request id. A bank calls back when a credit fails.

body.x: The amount is in paise and comes with the request, but it is checked against what the payer approved; a repeat of the same request id with a different amount is refused, not treated as a new payment.

Payer apps call an API gateway (a limit per app), then a load balancer, then the switch: stateless servers in three zones. The switch saves the payment in one database, by request id, then puts the two bank calls on a queue. Bank workers take them from the queue, call the banks, and write the result. A bank's callback comes back through the same gateway to the same switch. The database is sharded and has a standby in another zone.
Only the switch talks to the banks. Everything else asks the switch. That keeps one place that knows the state of every payment.

body.name: First try
body.what: Before debiting, look for a payment with the same amount to the same payee in the last minute.
body.avoid: It blocks a real second payment (two cups of chai) and misses a repeat that arrives later or through another path.
body.ex: Asha buys two ₹20 teas from the same stall, ten seconds apart. The second is refused.
body.like: A cashier who thinks every second purchase is a mistake.

body.name: Better
body.kind: A REQUEST ID, UNIQUE IN THE DATABASE
body.what: The app makes one request id per payment and sends it with every retry. The database refuses a second row with the same request id, so a repeat finds the first payment and returns it.
body.use: Any number of retries, from any path, lead to one payment and at most one debit.
body.avoid: A real second payment needs a new request id: the app makes one only after the first is known to have ended.
body.ex: The retry for rq_3 finds tx_3, already pending, and simply returns its status.
body.like: A receipt number: showing it again does not buy the item again.

items: When a bank does not answer in time, the payment is pending, not failed. The money may have moved.
The app asks for the status with the same request id, and the switch asks the bank by the same transaction id until it gets an answer.
Never show failed for a payment that may have succeeded: the payer will pay again.
Calls to the banks carry the transaction id, so a bank that gets the same call twice can recognise it.
If the debit worked and the credit failed, the switch marks the payment reversed and records a reversal in the same database transaction. Either both happen or neither.
The bank worker then asks the payer's bank to return the money, with the reversal's own id so a repeat is harmless.
A payment can be reversed only if it is still debited: the status change has a condition, so a late duplicate callback does nothing.
Reversals are added, never edited. At the end of the day the switch compares its records with each bank's report and adds correcting entries for any gap.
Size the switch and the database for the peak, not the average: salary day arrives in minutes and no one can add servers that fast.
The queue absorbs the bank calls. A slow bank makes the queue longer; it does not make starting a payment slower.
A per-app limit at the gateway stops one app that retries wildly from using the capacity everyone else needs.
If one bank is down, payments to and from it wait in the queue and finish when it is back; other banks are not affected.
Junior / mid: a switch with a database and a queue; a request id that makes a retry safe; pending as a state.
Senior: reversals in the same transaction; unknown results; peak sizing; a standby database in another zone.
Staff: per-bank queues and limits; daily reconciliation; how the switch proves it never took money twice.
"One bank is slow?" A queue and a limit per bank, so its backlog cannot use the workers the other banks need.
"A bank calls back twice?" The status change is conditional, so the second call finds the payment already changed and does nothing.
"How do you find a payment that is stuck?" A job that lists payments pending for longer than the bank's time limit and asks the bank about each by its transaction id.
"How do you test it?" A fault test for each step: a bank down, a bank slow, a zone lost, the database failing over, a status-check storm.

body.x: Like a payment, a saved order is a promise: it must not vanish when a part crashes. The lost-orders challenge practises keeping that promise.

practice.brief: Each test sends UPI payments from the payer apps and the apps' status checks after a timeout (7 in 10 and 3 in 10), and the banks call back when a credit fails. A payment must never be debited twice, and a debit that did not reach the payee must be reversed.

steps.label: Asking the banks to debit and credit

operations.name: A bank says the credit failed

tests.name: Pay ₹480 to Zotato
tests.desc: Ravi pays Zotato ₹480 (tx_3). The payment is saved once, by the app's request id, as pending; the banks are asked afterwards, so the app is not kept waiting on them.

tests.name: The app checks a payment
tests.desc: A timeout makes the app ask what happened to its request rq_1. It reads the saved payment and answers; it never starts a second one.

tests.name: A bank says the credit failed
tests.desc: The payee's bank cannot credit tx_2. In one transaction the payment is marked reversed and a reversal is added, so the payer's money goes back exactly once.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 1,000 requests a second from the payer apps, and the banks' callbacks.

tests.name: Salary day, 10 am
tests.desc: 3,000 requests a second on the 1st of the month. Nothing may be debited twice or lost.

tests.name: The festival-sale rush
tests.desc: At 8 pm a sale starts: 8,000 requests a second for 15 minutes.

tests.name: A bank goes down
tests.desc: At 10:10 am a bank stops answering for 10 minutes. Payers can still start payments; the banks are asked again when it is back.

tests.name: A bank slows down
tests.desc: At 10:10 am the banks take ten times as long to answer, for 15 minutes. Starting a payment must stay fast; the banks may catch up within 30 minutes.

tests.name: The status-check storm
tests.desc: At 10:10 am a timeout makes one app send four times its traffic for 15 minutes, asking again and again. Everyone else must still be able to pay.

tests.name: A zone goes dark
tests.desc: At 10:10 am one availability zone is lost for 15 minutes. Payments may slow down; none may be lost.

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (1,000 a second), storage and data transfer included. Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails.

wrong.name: No request id check
wrong.why: Nothing stops a second debit for the same request id: a retry becomes a second payment.

wrong.name: Reversals in another database
wrong.why: The payment and its reversal land in two databases: no transaction spans them, so a crash can leave money taken and not returned.

wrong.name: Banks cannot call back
wrong.why: Nothing connects the banks to the switch, so a failed credit is never heard of and the debit is never reversed.

wrong.name: The payer waits for the banks
wrong.why: The switch asks the banks before it answers: when a bank is down, nobody can even start a payment.

wrong.name: Sized for a normal day
wrong.why: The switch and its database fit an ordinary afternoon, not the festival-sale rush.

wrong.name: One zone
wrong.why: Every part of the switch is in one zone: when it goes dark, nothing answers.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: The database has no standby: when it crashes, payments stop for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Write-back cache in front of the transactions
wrong.why: The cache confirms payments and saves them later: a crash loses debits the payer was told succeeded.

wrong.name: No limit per client
wrong.why: The gateway lets one app send as much as it likes: a status-check storm starves everyone else.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: It passes every test, at several times the bill it needs.

decisions.q: The phone sends the same payment twice after a timeout. How do you not debit twice?
options: Compare the amount and payee with the last payment, and refuse a match
A request id the database keeps unique, so a repeat finds the first
Debit both, then reverse the second one in the nightly check
decisions.why: A timeout does not say whether the first request worked, so the phone must be free to repeat it. A unique request id makes the repeat return the first result. Matching on amount blocks real second payments, and reversing later still takes the money twice.

decisions.q: A bank does not answer in time. What does the payer see?
options: Success, so the payer is not kept waiting at all
Failed, so the payer can try again straight away
Pending, until the bank answers or the switch asks it
decisions.why: Not answering is not failing: the money may have moved. Pending (checked later, with the same transaction id) is the only honest answer; failed invites a second payment, and success may be false.

decisions.q: The payer's bank debited but the payee's bank could not credit. What fixes it?
options: A reversal saved with the status change, in one transaction
Ask the payer to raise a complaint with their bank
Credit the payee from the switch's own money, then settle later
decisions.why: The reversal must happen exactly once and must not be forgotten if the switch crashes: that needs the status change and the reversal record in one transaction, and its own id so the bank can drop a repeat.

decisions.q: Salary day sends three times the traffic. What do you do?
options: Size for the average, and add servers by hand if the day needs them
Turn away payments above a fixed rate until the peak has passed
Size for the peak, and queue the bank calls so a spike adds wait only there
decisions.why: The peak arrives faster than anyone can add servers, and the banks cannot be made faster. Sizing the switch for the peak and absorbing the bank calls in a queue keeps starting a payment quick.

hints.x: A UPI payment moves money between two banks you do not run. What must be true even when a bank is slow, down, or answers twice?
Work from a model month-start: how many payments a second at 10 am on the 1st, and how many of those are repeats and status checks?
The payer's phone sends a transaction id with every payment. Which calls does it make, and which one is safe to repeat?
Save the payment first, by its transaction id. A second request with the same id must find the first, not start another.
The banks are slow and not yours: put a Queue between the switch and its bank workers, so a slow bank costs time, not payments.
A failed credit has to reverse the debit once. Write the status change and the reversal in one transaction, in the same database as the payment, with a standby in another zone.

practice.referenceNote: Every payment is saved once, by its transaction id, before any bank is asked. The banks are asked from a queue, so a slow or absent bank does not hold up the payer. A failed credit and the reversal are written in one transaction.
